title: Bats Use Echoes to See
summary: How many bats find their way and catch insects in the dark by listening to echoes, why they are not blind, and how they help farms and wild plants, including in Saudi Arabia.
poll: Bats are more helpful to people than most people think.

versions.title: Bats Hear in the Dark
versions.text:
It is night. The sky is dark. A bat flies out to eat.

A bat is a mammal. It has fur. Its young drink milk. But a bat can fly! Its wings are thin skin on long bones.

How can a bat find bugs in the dark? It yells. The sound is too high for us to hear. The sound hits a bug. Then it bounces back. That is an echo.

The bat hears the echo. The echo tells it where the bug is. It tells it how big the bug is, too. Then the bat zips in and grabs it.

Bats are not blind. All bats can see. Some big bats eat fruit. They find it with their eyes and nose.

Bats help us. One small bat can eat lots of insects in one night. Some of the bugs hurt crops. Fruit bats help, too. They drop seeds. New trees grow.

Bats live in Saudi Arabia, too. They hide in caves and old homes in the day.

versions.title: Seeing with Sound
versions.text:
When the sun sets, many bats wake up and leave their caves to hunt. The evening is dark, and the insects they eat are tiny. So how do these flying animals manage to capture them?

Bats are mammals, like camels and cats, because they have fur and feed their babies milk. But bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. Their wings are made of thin skin stretched over very long finger bones.

Many bats find their prey with a special skill called echolocation. As a bat flies, it sends out short, high calls. Most of these sounds are too high in pitch for people to hear. When a call hits an object, the sound bounces back as an echo. The bat listens to the echo to learn where the object is, how big it is, and which direction it is moving. As the bat comes closer to a moth, it calls faster and faster until it catches its dinner.

Bats are not blind. Every bat can actually see. Many large fruit bats find their food mostly with their eyes and their sense of smell.

People have copied this clever idea. Ships use a tool called sonar, which sends sound through the water and listens for echoes to locate the bottom of the ocean or groups of fish.

Bats are useful to people, too. A small bat can eat hundreds of insects in one night, including pests that damage crops. Some bats pollinate flowers, and fruit bats spread seeds that grow into new trees.

Several different kinds of bats live in Saudi Arabia. During the day, they rest in caves, rocky valleys, and empty buildings.

versions.title: Listening to the Night: How Bats Use Echoes
versions.text:
As the sun sets, many bats awaken and emerge from their caves to hunt, but the evening is dark and the insects they eat are minuscule, so how do these flying mammals manage to capture them so successfully?

Bats belong to the same animal group as camels and cats, and the mothers nurse their babies with milk. However, bats are the only mammals capable of true flight, and their wings consist of thin, elastic skin stretched over extremely long finger bones. With more than 1,400 known species, bats make up approximately one out of every five kinds of mammals on Earth.

Many bats navigate and hunt using an ability called echolocation. As a bat flies, it produces short calls that are mostly ultrasonic, meaning their frequency is too high for human ears to detect. When a call strikes an object, the sound bounces back as an echo. By analyzing these echoes, the animal determines the object's position, size, and direction of travel. As the hunter approaches a moth, it calls faster and faster, until the calls blur into a rapid buzz immediately before it captures its dinner.

The prey is not always defenseless, however, because some moths can detect approaching bats and dive toward the ground to escape their predator, and a few even produce clicks of their own that seem to confuse or warn the hunter.

Contrary to a popular myth, bats are not blind; every bat can see. Many large fruit bats depend primarily on their eyesight and excellent sense of smell to discover food.

Humans have imitated this ingenious technique: ships use sonar, a device that sends sound through the water and listens for echoes to locate the ocean floor or schools of fish.

Bats are also valuable to people. A single small bat can consume hundreds of insects in one evening, including pests that damage agricultural crops, while other bats pollinate flowers or scatter seeds.

Several different species inhabit Saudi Arabia, sheltering in caves, rocky valleys, and abandoned buildings during the day.

versions.title: Listening to the Night: The Science of Echolocation
versions.text:
As the sun sets, many bats awaken and emerge from their caves to hunt. The evening is dark and the insects they consume are minuscule, so how do these airborne mammals manage to capture them with such remarkable consistency?

Bats belong to the same animal group as camels and cats, and the mothers nurse their offspring with milk. Nevertheless, bats are the only mammals capable of genuine powered flight, and their wings consist of thin, elastic membranes stretched over extraordinarily elongated finger bones. With more than 1,400 identified species, bats represent approximately one out of every five varieties of mammals on Earth.

Many bats navigate and hunt using an ability called echolocation. As a bat flies, it produces brief vocalizations that are predominantly ultrasonic, meaning their frequency is too high for human ears to detect. When a call strikes an object, the sound reflects back as an echo, and by analyzing these echoes, the animal determines the object's position, size, and direction of travel. As the hunter approaches an insect, it vocalizes with increasing rapidity, until the calls blur into a continuous buzz immediately before it captures its dinner.

The prey is not always defenseless, however, because certain moths can detect approaching bats and plunge toward the ground to escape their predator, and some even produce clicking sounds of their own that appear to confuse or warn the hunter, an interaction that scientists consider an evolutionary competition between predator and prey.

Contrary to a widespread misconception, bats are not blind; every bat can see. Many large fruit bats depend primarily on their eyesight and exceptionally sensitive sense of smell to discover food.

Humans have imitated this ingenious biological technique: ships utilize sonar, a device that transmits sound through the water and listens for echoes to locate the ocean floor or schools of fish.

Bats are also economically valuable, because a single small bat can consume hundreds of insects in one evening, including pests that damage agricultural crops, while other species pollinate flowers or disperse seeds that regenerate forests.

Several different species inhabit Saudi Arabia, sheltering in caves, rocky valleys, and abandoned buildings during the daytime.

versions.title: Listening to the Night: The Science of Echolocation
versions.text:
As the sun sets, many bats awaken and emerge from their caves to hunt; the evening is dark and the insects they consume are minuscule, so how do these airborne mammals manage to capture them with such remarkable consistency?

Bats belong to the same zoological category as camels and cats, and the mothers nurse their offspring with milk; nevertheless, bats are the only mammals capable of genuine powered flight, and their wings consist of thin, elastic membranes stretched over extraordinarily elongated finger bones. With more than 1,400 identified species, bats represent approximately one out of every five varieties of mammals on Earth.

Many bats navigate and hunt using an ability called echolocation. As a bat flies, it produces brief vocalizations that are predominantly ultrasonic, meaning their frequency is too high for human ears to detect. When a call strikes an object, the sound reflects back as an echo, and by analyzing these echoes, the animal determines the object's position, size, and direction of travel. As the hunter approaches an insect, it vocalizes with increasing rapidity, until the individual calls blur into a continuous buzz immediately before it captures its dinner.

The prey is not always defenseless, however, because certain moths can detect approaching bats and plunge toward the ground to escape their predator, and some even produce clicking sounds of their own that apparently confuse or warn the hunter, an interaction that scientists consider an evolutionary competition between predator and prey that has continued for millions of years.

Contrary to a widespread misconception, bats are not blind; every bat can see. Many large fruit bats depend primarily on their eyesight and exceptionally sensitive sense of smell to discover food.

Humans have imitated this ingenious biological technique: ships utilize sonar, a device that transmits sound through the water and listens for echoes to locate the ocean floor or schools of fish.

Bats are also economically valuable. A single small bat can consume hundreds of insects in one evening, including pests that damage agricultural crops, while other species pollinate flowers or disperse seeds that regenerate forests.

Several different species inhabit Saudi Arabia, sheltering in caves, rocky valleys, and abandoned buildings during the daytime. One of them, the Egyptian fruit bat, is unusual among fruit bats because it produces echolocation clicks using its tongue.

MID.prompt: The article says people copied the bats' trick to build sonar. Explain how echolocation and sonar are alike and different, using details from the article.
checklist: I described at least one way they are alike.
I described at least one way they are different.
I used the words echolocation and sonar correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: Echolocation and sonar are alike because both send out sound and then listen for an echo bouncing back off something, whether it is a flying insect that is prey for a bat or a school of fish under the water. They are different because a bat uses extremely high-pitched calls at a pitch human ears cannot even detect, while sonar on a ship sends sound through water instead of air to find the ocean floor or fish. People actually copied the bat's echolocation trick when they invented sonar, which shows how useful this hunting method is, even though some bats also pollinate flowers using their eyesight and sense of smell instead.

HIGH.prompt: Some people fear bats. Write a paragraph that would persuade them that bats deserve protection, using at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I stated a clear opinion in my first sentence.
I supported it with at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
I used precise words such as predator, species, or navigate.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Bats deserve far more protection than people usually give them. First, many species of bats are incredibly helpful predators that eat hundreds of insects in a single night, including pests that would otherwise damage farmers' crops. Second, bats use ultrasonic sound at a frequency to navigate and hunt in complete darkness through echolocation, an ability so remarkable that humans copied it to invent sonar for finding objects underwater. Third, some bats pollinate flowers and scatter seeds that grow into new trees, which means they quietly help forests and farms regrow. Bats are not the frightening creatures of scary stories; they are intelligent, essential animals that deserve our protection, not our fear.
